name: configurable-test-double
intent: Configure one reusable Test Double per collaborator role during fixture setup - before the test installs it in the system under test - so the values it returns and the calls it expects are stated as configuration data in the test itself instead of being hard-coded into a purpose-built double class per scenario.
problem: Several tests need the same collaborator role (clock, gateway, repository, notifier) to behave differently: some need canned successes, others exceptions, timeouts or specific call arguments. When every variation is its own hard-coded double class, the suite duplicates double code and the configured behaviour is buried inside the double rather than visible in the test, which is Meszaros' Test Code Duplication and Obscure Tests territory.
context: Unit tests that isolate a system under test by replacing a depended-on component, where the same collaborator role recurs across many tests with slightly different data or failure modes and a substitutable-dependency seam (constructor or parameter injection, factory, registry, subclass hook) exists to install the double. It covers both construction routes - a hand-built reusable double and a toolkit that statically or dynamically generates one - and both configuration styles, a test-only configuration interface or a record/playback configuration mode.
benefits: One double implementation serves many tests: per-test variation becomes configuration data, so the duplicated double class per scenario disappears.
The configured values sit in the test next to the assertion that depends on them, so a reader sees what the collaborator was told to do instead of hunting through a double class.
Failure paths - exceptions, timeouts, error codes, empty results - are injected by configuration, without writing a new double for each failure mode.
A mistake in the double is fixed once, for every test that uses it, and the double is maintained in a single place.

Generated or dynamically created doubles remove the boilerplate and can be restricted to the real collaborator's API (spec'd, autospec'd or verifying doubles), which turns a typo or a removed method into a failure instead of a silently vacuous test.
The same double acts as control point and observation point: indirect inputs are configured and indirect outputs are recorded or asserted through one object.
Configuration data can be parameterized and driven by external data sources (CSV, JSON), enabling data-driven test scenarios without code duplication.
When combined with contract testing (e.g., Pact), configured doubles verify consumer-side interactions match the provider's actual contract, catching drift before it breaks production.
tradeoffs: Configuration is a second surface that can drift from the real collaborator: a double configured with impossible values, or an expectation on a method that no longer exists, can leave a broken production path green.
A reusable double carries mutable configured state; unless it is re-created or reset during fixture setup the state leaks into the next test and failures become order-dependent.
Over-specified expectations turn the double into a specification of the implementation, producing fragile tests that break on refactoring rather than on behaviour changes.
Generated doubles hide what is substituted: an unspec'd dynamic double accepts almost any call, so a test can pass while exercising nothing.
Indirection while reading: the test shows configuration calls rather than the double's behaviour, and the configuration API of the toolkit or double must itself be learned.
For a single test the configuration surface costs more than hard-coding a one-off double, and every extra configuration method is test infrastructure that must be maintained.

Toolkits that generate doubles at runtime need reflection or bytecode instrumentation, and generators need a build step, which adds build complexity and constrains what can be doubled (final or sealed types, value types, inline functions).

Mocking frameworks can create a false sense of security: tests may pass because the double was correctly configured rather than because the production code correctly handles the real collaborator's behaviour.
Nested mocking (double returning another double) obscures the call chain and produces uninterpretable failure messages.

participants.responsibility: Test-specific implementation of the depended-on component that holds the values to return and the calls to expect; the system under test reaches it only through the production interface.
Test-only methods - per-value setters, constructor parameters or a fluent/generic expectation builder - that install the responses and expected arguments before the double is used.
The installed return values, raised failures and expected arguments that the double replays while the test exercises the system under test.
Creates, configures and installs the double during the fixture-setup phase of the four-phase test, and re-configures or re-creates it for each test so no state leaks.
The code being tested, which calls the double through the production interface and is unaware that a configuration interface exists.
Optional alternative to a separate configuration interface: the double is put into a record/teach state during setup and switched to playback before the system under test runs.
Optional participant that fabricates the double for the test, statically by code generation or dynamically through reflection and proxies, so no double class is written by hand.
The substitutable-dependency seam (constructor injection, factory, setter, registry, subclass hook) through which the configured double replaces the real collaborator.

use_cases: A collaborator role used by many tests with different canned answers - time provider, pricing or tax service, identifier generator, feature-flag client - where only the returned value varies between tests.

Injecting failures on demand: the double is configured per test to raise timeouts, throw exceptions or return error codes so the error-handling paths of the system under test are exercised without a second double class.
Verifying indirect outputs: expected arguments are configured on the same double and the test asserts afterwards that the right message was sent with the right payload.
A suite-wide fixture double for a slow, unavailable or side-effecting dependency, re-configured per test instead of re-implemented per test.
Generated doubles for collaborators with wide interfaces, where hand-writing a double class would be pure boilerplate and would have to be kept in step with the interface.
Cutting a deep chain of real collaborators during refactoring: one configured double stands in for the chain so fixture setup stops constructing and persisting a network of objects.

Contract testing with external services: configure a double to return contract-compliant responses that verify the system under test produces correctly-formatted requests (see Pact, consumer-driven contracts).
Testing async/await code paths: configure the double to return awaitable results or throw exceptions asynchronously, exercising the calling code's async error handling.
Performance boundary testing: configure a double with deliberate delays or throttling to verify timeout and retry logic behaves correctly under degraded conditions.
State machine testing across transitions: configure the double to return specific state-dependent responses as the system under test walks through a sequence of transitions.
Consumer-driven contract verification: use a mock server (e.g., Pact mock) to record expected interactions, generating a contract that the provider can verify independently.
Testing retry and circuit-breaker logic: configure the double to fail a configurable number of times before succeeding, exercising back-off and recovery paths.
Data-driven test scenarios: parameterize the double's configuration with external data (CSV, JSON) to cover many input combinations without duplicating test code.

Java suites configure one Mockito mock per collaborator interface - when(clock.now()).thenReturn(instant) for indirect inputs, verify(gateway).send(msg) for indirect outputs - replacing hand-built double classes.

Python tests install unittest.mock.patch(..., autospec=True) or create_autospec(...) doubles per test, configuring return_value/side_effect and asserting calls via assert_called_with, with signatures checked against the real object.

Go tests run mockgen (uber-go/mock) over the collaborator interface once and configure expectations during setup - mockFoo.EXPECT().Bar(gomock.Eq(99)).Return(101).Times(1) - since Go offers no runtime proxying.
avoid_when: The double is needed by exactly one test with one behaviour: a hard-coded test double - an anonymous class, lambda or local function - is simpler and keeps the behaviour visible at the point of use.
The parameter is required but never used by this path: a Dummy Object or a null placeholder is enough, no configuration needed.
A working but cheap implementation already expresses the intent (in-memory repository, fake clock): a Fake Object carries the behaviour and needs no configuration surface.
The real collaborator is fast, deterministic and side-effect-free in the test environment: use the real object and keep it in the suite as the test that catches double/reality drift.
The interaction sequence itself is the behaviour under test and a plain per-test expectation already expresses it: extra configurability adds a surface without adding information.
The project's existing framework already provides per-test stubbing with the same reuse; building a parallel configuration interface on top duplicates the machinery.
The test requires mocking too many collaborators (typically more than 3-5): this signals tight coupling and the design should be refactored before masking it with doubles.
anti_patterns: Test logic in production: the configuration interface, or a test-only mode flag, leaking into the production interface so production callers can re-configure the collaborator.
A reusable double kept in shared fixture state without reset, so configured responses and recorded calls leak between tests and failures become order-dependent.
A configuration surface that mirrors every member of the collaborator, turning the double into a second, unreadable copy of the interface.
Configuring the double to return values the real collaborator can never produce and treating the green test as evidence about production behaviour.
Replacing the very component under test with a configurable double, so the test verifies the double's configuration rather than the system under test.
Unspec'd dynamic doubles that accept calls to methods which no longer exist, letting interface changes rot the suite silently.

Over-specified expectations: asserting exact call arguments, call counts, or call order when only the fact of the call matters to the behaviour under test, producing tests that break on implementation refactoring.
Nested mocking: configuring a double to return another mock, creating an implicit chain of test doubles that hides what is actually being exercised and makes failure messages uninterpretable.
Over-mocking: using many mocks in a single test, which masks tight coupling and produces brittle tests that require constant maintenance as implementation changes.
Mocking concrete classes without interfaces, coupling tests directly to implementation details and causing widespread test failures on routine refactoring.
Mocking types you don't own without an adapter layer, violating the principle of only testing against stable, owned contracts.
design_principles: Separation of concerns, backed by interface segregation: the production interface stays minimal while the test-only configuration interface carries the configurability.
Dependency inversion: the system under test depends on the collaborator's abstraction, which is what allows a configured double to stand in for the real implementation.
Don't repeat yourself: one double implementation configured per test instead of one double class per test.
Open/closed principle: a new test scenario is a new configuration of the existing double, not a modification or subclass of it.
Information hiding: the system under test must not know that its collaborator is a double, nor that a configuration interface exists on it.
Single responsibility: the double only provides controlled behaviour; assertions, intent and expected outcomes stay in the test.
Interface segregation for test doubles: mock or stub interfaces rather than concrete classes to avoid coupling tests to implementation details.
Own what you mock: wrap third-party or external dependencies in an adapter you control, and mock the adapter rather than the external code directly.
best_practices: Configure the double during fixture setup, before installing it into the system under test, and keep the configuration next to the assertion it serves.
Re-create or explicitly reset the double's configured state for every test; never share a mutable configurable double through a static or suite-wide fixture.
Prefer doubles that are checked against the real collaborator (verifying doubles, spec'd or autospec'd mocks, generated mocks) so typos and removed members fail loudly.
Configure only what the test depends on and give the rest a default that fails the test rather than a catch-all that accepts any call.
Keep at least one test that runs the system under test against the real collaborator, or a full integration test, to catch drift between the double and reality.
Never let the configuration interface become part of the production API, and never configure a double to return values the real collaborator cannot produce.
When the double needs real behaviour - a store, a call log, a lightweight algorithm - implement a fake with that logic inside it instead of piling conditional configuration onto a mock.

Prefer the simplest form of double that meets the test's need: use a stub for indirect inputs, a mock for behaviour verification, and only escalate to a full configurable double when multiple tests need different configurations of the same collaborator.
When using a mocking toolkit, prefer argument matchers (any(), eq(), contains()) over hardcoded values for arguments the test does not care about, to reduce over-specification and brittleness.
Use configuration objects or named constants instead of magic values when configuring return values, so test intent is self-documenting.
Document the reason for a specific configuration in the test name or a brief comment, especially when configuring unusual, unexpected, or edge-case values.
Isolate fixture setup into well-named factory methods or test data builders when the same double configuration is reused across multiple tests, keeping individual tests readable.
Mock interfaces, not concrete classes: this enforces dependency inversion and prevents tests from breaking on implementation refactoring that does not change behaviour.
Wrap third-party dependencies in an adapter before mocking: mock the adapter interface rather than the third-party class directly, so contract changes in the library are isolated to the adapter.

For async methods, use the framework's async-aware mock (AsyncMock in Python, ReturnsAsync/ThrowsAsync in Moq) and always await the result in tests; never use a synchronous mock for an async collaborator.
Limit the number of mocks per test to 3-5 maximum; more indicates tight coupling and a need to refactor the design rather than mask it with doubles.
Combine with a Test Data Builder to construct complex configured states cleanly: the builder produces the data the double will return or verify.
When verifying interactions, assert on the meaningful behaviour (was the right method called?) rather than on exact argument equality for every parameter; use matchers for irrelevant fields.
Use a contract testing framework (e.g., Pact) alongside configurable doubles to ensure the double's configured behaviour stays aligned with the real provider's contract.
sources: Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code (Addison-Wesley, 2007) - Chapter 23, Configurable Test Double (p. 558) and its variations: Configuration Interface, Configuration Mode, Hand-Built, Statically and Dynamically Generated Test Doubles; Hard-Coded Test Double (p. 568).

https://martinfowler.com/articles/mocksArentStubs.html - Martin Fowler's classic article distinguishing mocks from stubs, covering classical vs mockist TDD styles and state vs behaviour verification.
https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ObjectMother.html - Martin Fowler's Object Mother pattern, a factory-based approach for creating test objects that complements configurable test doubles.
https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDouble.html - Martin Fowler's glossary entry introducing Meszaros's Test Double taxonomy (Dummy, Fake, Stub, Spy, Mock) as the standard vocabulary.

https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ContractTest.html - Martin Fowler's contract testing article explaining how test doubles for external services should be verified against real behaviour through contract tests.
http://xunitpatterns.com - The xUnit Patterns website, the online companion to Meszaros's book, with expanded content and additional patterns.
Steve Dunn, 'Prefer test-doubles over mocking frameworks' (dunnhq.com, 2024) - argues for hand-written test doubles over mocking frameworks for clearer, more robust tests.
Vinted Engineering, 'The Downsides of Excessive Mocks (framework) and Stubs' (vinted.engineering, 2023) - documents real-world costs of over-mocking including test fragility and design distortion.

Nat Pryce, 'Test Data Builders: an alternative to the Object Mother pattern' (natpryce.com, 2007) - the original article introducing Test Data Builders as a more flexible alternative to Object Mother for constructing test objects.

https://blog.szymonmiks.pl - 'Test Doubles in Python unit tests' (2024) - practical guide covering unittest.mock usage, the 'don't mock what you don't own' principle, and configurable test doubles in Python.
Microsoft, 'Mocking in Unit Tests - Engineering Fundamentals Playbook' (microsoft.github.io, 2024) - enterprise guidance on when and how to use test doubles and mocking frameworks effectively.

Google Testing Blog, 'Testing on the Toilet: Don't Overuse Mocks' (testing.googleblog.com, 2013) - warns against excessive mocking that duplicates production logic, increases complexity, and signals tight coupling.

Robert C. Martin, 'Mocking Mocking and Testing Outcomes' (sites.google.com/site/unclebobconsultingllc) - argues that mocking frameworks should be used sparingly and tests should focus on outcomes over method-call verification.
Pact Docs, 'Introduction' (docs.pact.io) - consumer-driven contract testing framework that uses configured test doubles (mocks) to generate contracts verified against real providers.
The Runtime, 'Testing Async Code in .NET: Patterns and Pitfalls' (the-runtime.dev, 2025) - async testing patterns with mocks including ThrowsAsync, ReturnsAsync, and common async testing pitfalls.
DEV Community, 'How to Test Async Python Code with pytest-asyncio' (dev.to, 2025) - using AsyncMock for async method doubles and proper awaiting in async tests.

Software Patterns Lexicon, 'Java Mocking and Stubs for Pattern Collaborators' (softwarepatternslexicon.com, 2024) - guidance on applying test doubles to GoF pattern testing, covering Proxy, Strategy, and Adapter relationships.
CodeClarityLab, 'Mocking Best Practices (PHPUnit & Mockery)' (codeclaritylab.com, 2025) - mock interfaces not concrete classes, distinguish stubs from mocks, don't mock what you don't own.

Philippe Bourgau, 'How to use Test Data Builders to avoid mocks and keep your tests clear' (philippe.bourgau.net, 2023) - Test Data Builders as an alternative to over-mocking for complex test data scenarios.

http://xunitpatterns.com/Configurable%20Test%20Double.html - Meszaros's Configurable Test Double pattern page on xunitpatterns.com: configuration during fixture setup, Configuration Interface vs Configuration Mode, Hard-Coded vs Configurable doubles.

https://site.mockito.org/ - Mockito official documentation: when(...).thenReturn(...)/thenThrow(...) stubbing and verify(...) expectations on generated mocks, the canonical dynamically-generated configurable double for Java.

https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.mock.html - Python unittest.mock official documentation: patch with autospec and create_autospec produce signature-verifying doubles configured per test via return_value/side_effect.

https://github.com/uber-go/mock/blob/main/README.md - GoMock (uber-go/mock) README: mockgen statically generates configurable mock implementations of Go interfaces; expectations recorded with EXPECT()/Return()/Times() during setup.

AndroidX team, 'Do Not Mock' (android.googlesource.com/platform/frameworks/support) - the Jetpack team's guidance against mocking frameworks in library tests: mocks break API guarantees and make tests brittle; prefer real instances and observable outcomes.
